grid.text: Disease, problem or Condition under investigation
Patients with active cancer and acute proximal deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism who had completed at least 6 months of anticoagulant therapy.

Risks were similar between sexes, 4 but sex itself could be a confounding factor with the site of cancer (e.g., breast, prostate, colorectal, lung). Age was not found to be an independent risk factor for VTE during the initial treatment phase 5 but it could be a

recurrent confounding factor with the site of cancer; a pancreatic or hepatobiliary cancer site was associated with a higher risk of recurrence. Different cancer sites impact venous thromboembolic risk and treatment outcomes. Hence, cancer

site may influence both the age effect and treatment response. One major risk factor for cancer-associated thrombosis is ethnicity, 6,7 but there are no data on the risk of recurrence of venous thromboembolism. Owing to legal constraints in France, no data were collected on race and ethnicity in this trial. Therefore, it is not possible to comment on the representativeness of our study with respect to specific racial and ethnic groups.

Age, ethnicity, and sites of cancer vary across countries. All these factors may be confounding. However, to our knowledge, there is no known geographical variation in venous thromboembolism recurrence in cancer patients.

Since the study enrolled patients with cancer (66% of patients have metastatic disease), the incidence of risk factors differs from patients without cancer (18% with a history of VTE), and most events are pulmonary embolism.

The API-CAT trial included patients with a wide spectrum of cancers representative of current clinical practice. The study population is reflective of individuals undergoing extended treatment in routine clinical practice, in terms of their age, cancer type, and cancer stage. Their baseline characteristics are similar to those seen in observational studies and randomized trials. 8-10
